#1
ĐANG HỌC
I’ve always been drawn to the uncanny -- the slightly creepy.
#2
I make movies about spiders playing jazz on their webs,
#3
or cockroaches building a rocket
#4
to fly to the moon and explore the universe.
#5
I love finding the human in what most people find a bit creepy.
#6
So when the first AI images like this appeared,
#7
I was not creeped out.
#8
I was really curious.
#9
What new ways of filmmaking could this unlock?
#10
I started a YouTube channel to find out.
#11
Some of my early experiments were nature documentaries
#12
generated using one of the earliest AI-video models.
#13
It was so early that it couldn't even remember
#14
what happened half a second ago,
#15
which is why it looks like planet Earth on acid --
#16
I imagine, I mean, I wouldn’t know.
#17
(Laughter)
#18
My favorite early project, though,
#19
was using, back at the time, cutting-edge AI tools
#20
to generate the story, the 3D models
#21
and even the animation
#22
to create a sequel to my favorite Pixar movie,
#23
"Ratatouille," of course.
#24
And it became whatever this is:
#25
(Video) Gusteau always said that anyone can cook,
#26
but only the fearless can be great.
#27
(Dramatic music)
#28
Oh! Help! Help me, Remy!
#29
(Screaming)
#30
(Evil cackle)
#31
Mick Mahler: So, yeah.
#32
(Laughter)
#33
Not exactly Hollywood, I know,
#34
but I really loved pushing these tools to their limits
#35
to see where they'd break.
#36
And as you can see -- they broke pretty fast.
#37
But now AI can make almost anything I can imagine,
#38
and it’s getting better and easier to use every single day.
#39
That’s amazing, but also kind of terrifying, right?
#40
I mean, what happens when everything becomes possible?
#41
Will anyone be able to just prompt a Hollywood blockbuster now?
#42
Or will we drown in an ocean of meaningless AI-generated content --
#43
what we now call “AI slop.”
#44
I'm actually more optimistic.
#45
And to show you why, I brought three projects that really inspired me.
#46
When a new AI model was released
#47
that could transform audio clips into animation,
#48
filmmakers from Berlin went out into the streets
#49
and interviewed pedestrians about their meat consumption,
#50
and then they used this AI model to transform their voices into this:
#51
(Video) I’d like to be a vegetarian. It affects my health.
#52
But yeah, I do feel better when I eat it.
#53
Alien 2: We need the meat because of our brains.
#54
Those things that are coming from the meat is helping the brains.
#55
(Laughter)
#56
Now, a lot of people are creating these over-the-top sci-fi movie trailers
#57
with explosions and stuff with AI.
#58
And I get that. That’s a lot of fun.
#59
But this stood out to me because it's not that.
#60
It's rooted in reality. It's a simple idea with a funny twist.
#61
And most importantly, it tells a story.
#62
That's how I like to approach my AI projects, too.
#63
Earlier this year, I felt really burnt out
#64
from sitting at my computer all day long, testing all these new AI models.
#65
I started to feel a bit like Gregor Samsa from Kafka's "The Metamorphosis."
#66
You know, the book about the guy who turns into this beetle creature.
#67
Well, inspired by that,
#68
I went outside and photographed real beetles,
#69
and then used these photos to train my own AI character model of this beetle.
#70
I then wrote an alternative ending for the story
#71
where Gregor, instead of dying alone miserably,
#72
reconnects with nature and learns that there's more to life than work.
#73
We then just went out into the woods and filmed this on an iPhone.
#74
(Laughter)
#75
And using this beetle model,
#76
I was able to transform myself into Gregor with just a few clicks.
#77
(Laughter)
#78
Meanwhile, people are now creating entire movies on their laptops.
#79
There's this growing community of filmmakers
#80
pushing the boundaries of AI,
#81
and to them, sharing how they made it matters as much as the final movie.
#82
And I think that openness is really cool.
#83
It really invites anyone to come in and join
#84
and start creating their own movies.
#85
So this is where we are right now.
#86
Soon anyone will be able to tell any story
#87
without technical limitations.
#88
So what happens when everything becomes possible?
#89
I think, yes, we're going to see amazing new aesthetics,
#90
new narrative forms we've never imagined
#91
and stories from people who couldn’t find their audience before.
#92
But we are also going to see --
#93
and we are already seeing -- a lot more trash:
#94
low-effort AI content to cut costs,
#95
deepfakes, misinformation [and] AI slop.
#96
But I think in that ocean of AI slop,
#97
authenticity stands out more than ever.
#98
Originality stands out. I think effort stands out.
#99
Remember the Studio Ghibli trend,
#100
when everyone turned themselves into these anime characters?
#101
It was everywhere online for a few weeks, then very quickly vanished
#102
because novelty creates hype, but gets boring fast.
#103
And I too was drawn to AI for the novelty,
#104
but the more perfect and easy to use these tools become,
#105
the more bored I am actually by the technology itself,
#106
and the more excited I become about the real question:
#107
What stories are we going to tell now?
#108
Because filmmakers were never remembered for their tools --
#109
they were remembered for their stories,
#110
for their ability to move audiences,
#111
for their vision.
#112
But I think here’s also the challenge,
#113
because the tools always kind of shaped that vision, right?
#114
When we didn't have sound, title cards became a whole art form.
#115
CGI is too expensive?
#116
Maybe we need to actually build a part of that set?
#117
Early AI looks weird and creepy?
#118
Lean into that and make abstract nightmare fuel
#119
to make people laugh.
#120
Now those constraints are fading, and to avoid getting lost,
#121
you have to be more sure than ever about what it is you want to create.
#122
I think when everything becomes possible,
#123
nothing matters more than your vision.
#124
So here is how I work now for my newer projects.
#125
For my newest short film about a man who changes size with his confidence,
#126
we went story first, tool second.
#127
We knew that AI would make the visual effects possible,
#128
so we just wrote it, went out and shot it,
#129
and then later we figured out our own AI workflow.
#130
[We] built an open-source model
#131
that you can run for free on your own computer --
#132
it’s very, very nerdy.
#133
That allowed us to control every creative decision.
#134
And that’s super important with AI -- to keep that control --
#135
because a lot of these AI tools
#136
will try to make creative decisions for you.
#137
Don't let them do that.
#138
Think about the story only you can tell.
#139
Make it weird, make it unique,
#140
so that no AI could generate it on its own.
#141
And if you want, use AI as a tool to reach that vision,
#142
but never to replace it.
#143
Animation voice: Thank you for your attention.
#144
Now go make something cool.
#145
MM: Sorry for that.
#146
(Laughter)
#147
Thank you.
#148
(Applause)
